beginner: The Fed isn't moving rates right now. The central bank is watching to see if inflation keeps falling toward 2% as expected, but tariffs and higher energy costs are creating headwinds that could slow the economy down.

The economy is growing but slowing. GDP growth just got revised down because tariffs are starting to bite, and that means businesses and consumers will feel the squeeze sooner than anyone thought three months ago.

Unemployment is stable at 4.4% and inflation is cooling, but geopolitical risk is real. The Middle East situation and policy uncertainty could derail the Fed's plan to gradually ease rates later this year.
moderate: Tariff pass-through is arriving faster than the Fed modeled. Q1 GDP growth revised down to 2.0% (from the 2.2% forecast) because energy and trade effects are compressing margins now, not later, forcing the Fed to stay patient on rate cuts despite core inflation running 2.41% in February.

The Fed's baseline assumes a soft landing: unemployment holds near 4.4%, core inflation edges toward 2% by year-end, and rates stay flat at 3.5% through 2026. That scenario requires tariff volatility to stabilize and Middle East tensions to ease, neither assured.

Real rates (policy rate minus inflation) remain restrictive at roughly 1.1%, weighing on capital investment and housing. The Fed won't cut unless inflation proves it can fall sustainably without recession, a bet that depends entirely on tariff implementation timelines.
expert: Core CPI at 2.41% in February with the Fed holding at 3.64% (real rate 1.23%) while Q1 GDP prints at 2.0% and tariff pass-through accelerates suggests the policy stance is shifting from neutral toward subtle tightening. The 0.2pp downward revision to full-year growth (now 2.3% vs. 2.5% baseline) signals tariffs are front-loading disinflation drag.

The Fed's baseline scenario requires core inflation to ease toward 2% by late 2026 while unemployment holds at current levels. Market repricing has already priced out two cuts that seemed probable in December, reflecting skepticism that tariff effects stay transitory and geopolitical tail risks remain contained.

Watch whether Q2 earnings guidance compresses faster than consensus expects. If companies start cutting employment or investment forecasts in May-June earnings season due to tariff cost pass-through, the unemployment forecast (4.2% year-end) becomes the binding constraint and forces an earlier rate cut cycle than the current 3.25% year-end guidance implies.

beginner: Canada's economy is in trouble. The country shrank in the fourth quarter and is growing slower than any year since COVID, while inflation has fallen so far (1.78%) that the central bank has room to cut rates if the economy gets worse.

US tariffs are hammering Canada's exports and hurting growth. The Bank of Canada is watching the damage unfold but can't cut aggressively because it needs to defend the currency against the falling economy and keep stability.

Unemployment is rising (6.74% in January) and the economy is weak, but inflation is incredibly low at 1.26% core. The central bank has ammunition to help but has to be careful about moving too fast without knowing how bad the tariff damage will be.
moderate: Canada's economy contracted 0.6% in Q4 2025 and grew only 1.7% for the full year (the weakest since the pandemic), yet the Bank of Canada held at 2.25% in March because US tariffs are driving capital outflows and currency weakness. Cutting rates now risks weakening the loonie further and importing inflation.

Headline inflation collapsed to 1.8% in February from 2.3% in January, with core falling to 1.1% (the slowest in five years), giving the BoC cover to ease. But the central bank faces a trilemma: cutting rates to boost growth risks capital flight, holding rates supports the currency but worsens recession odds, and tariff uncertainty makes both timing and magnitude unclear.

The unemployment rate of 6.74% and negative growth momentum suggest a BoC rate cut is coming, but only after tariff timelines crystallize. If US implementation accelerates or covers more sectors, expect emergency cuts. If negotiations stall tariffs, expect gradual easing to 1.75% by year-end alongside modest recovery.
expert: Canada's Q4 GDP contraction (0.6%) on top of 1.7% full-year growth with core inflation at 1.1% (February) means the BoC is undershooting its dual mandate on growth while having room on inflation. The 2.25% hold in March despite negative output gap signals currency defense trumps cyclical easing, a reversal from 2024 strategy.

Core CPI at 1.1% and unemployment trending toward 6.5%+ gives the BoC a 100-200bp cut corridor before it hits the zero-bound constraint, but capital account deterioration (tariff-driven investment pullback) means real rate policy space is narrower than nominal rates suggest. The BoC is implicitly targeting financial conditions tightness to stabilize FX despite domestic slack.

The forecast assumes 1.7% growth and 2.0% inflation year-end with the policy rate at 2.25%. If tariff revenue loss and corporate tax receipts accelerate fiscal tightening, and capital outflows exceed 50bp of currency depreciation per quarter, expect the BoC to cut to 1.75% by Q3 2026 and signal further easing. Watch April employment data and May tariff implementation detail for the trigger.

beginner: The UK is slowing down. Growth is getting weaker because of the Middle East war and because interest rates are staying higher than expected, making it harder for businesses and families to borrow and spend.

Inflation is still too high at 3.24% compared to the target of 2%, but it should come down as tariffs fade and energy prices stabilize. The Bank of England can start cutting rates once inflation is clearly heading lower.

The central bank is stuck: inflation remains sticky but growth is weak. Rate cuts are coming (probably 75 basis points this year), but the bank has to move slowly to avoid a currency crisis and keep inflation expectations from slipping.
moderate: Core inflation at 3.24% in February is still 1.2 points above target, but the BoE expects it to fall toward 2% as tariff pass-through and administered price impacts wane. Growth is slowing from 1.3% as Middle East tensions and delayed rate cuts hit confidence, setting up a classic UK dilemma: weak demand but sticky prices.

The BoE is forecast to cut by 75bp this year (from 3.75% today), but timing depends on inflation confirmation. The bank faces a real trade-off: cutting too fast risks sterling weakness and imported inflation, but cutting too slow suffocates growth when the output gap is already negative. Markets are pricing the first cut for May or June.

Watch core inflation over the next two quarters. If it falls decisively below 3% by June, the BoE will move aggressively on cuts. If it stalls or re-accelerates due to wage growth or energy volatility, expect a slower 50bp pace and pushback on growth forecasts from 1.5% to 1.0% or lower.
expert: Core CPI at 3.24% in February with the Bank of England holding at 3.75% and growth forecast at only 1.3% (down from prior guidance) reveals a deteriorating Phillips curve regime: inflation remains sticky despite negative output gap, forcing the BoE to sacrifice growth. The 75bp cut guidance for 2026 assumes tariff pass-through dissipates and energy prices stabilize by Q2.

Real rates (policy minus core inflation) are at 0.51%, the most restrictive in the G7, yet growth is weakest. This inversion signals either that equilibrium rates have fallen sharply or that near-term tail risks (sterling crash, wage-price spirals) are keeping the BoE defensive. The currency depreciation buffer from a weaker pound has evaporated since January.

The forecast path assumes 2.5% CPI year-end and 1.5% growth. If Q1 earnings data shows wage growth above 5% (March releases in May), expect BoE pushback on cut timing and a May hold followed by 50bp in June-August, stretching the cut cycle into 2027. Conversely, if May/June PMI falls below 48, expect an emergency 50bp cut and capitulation toward 1.25% by year-end.

beginner: Japan's economy barely avoided a recession. GDP grew just 0.2% in the fourth quarter, saved by household spending while exports and government spending stayed weak. The country is stuck in low-growth mode.

Inflation is still above the 2% target but is expected to fade later this year as the weaker yen effect wears off. The central bank has kept rates very low at 0.75% to try to boost growth, but it's not working yet.

Japan's real challenge is structural: an aging population, weak exports, and limited room for growth even if inflation falls. The central bank may nudge rates higher later in the year if inflation data allows, but it won't move fast because growth is fragile.
moderate: Japan's Q4 GDP rebounded 0.2% after a Q3 contraction, avoiding technical recession, but household spending is the only engine running while exports and government spending remain subdued. The 0.75% policy rate and consensus for near-2% inflation through mid-year suggest the central bank won't move until late 2026, when it may ease growth constraints by tightening slightly.

Headline inflation at 1.26% in February and core above 2% for the past two quarters masks an underlying trend that the Bank of Japan says is weaker. Imported price pressures from the weak yen are fading, and domestic wage growth is moderating, making the IMF's assumption of 2.2% inflation for 2026 and 2.3% for 2027 look optimistic relative to the BoJ's own guidance of below 2% by late 2026.

The BoJ is betting that disinflation resumes without another growth shock, allowing it to stay pat at 0.75% and signal future rate normalization. If Q1 earnings disappoint (May data) and companies cut capex or employment guidance, expect the central bank to hold through year-end and ratchet down inflation forecasts, pushing any tightening into 2027.
expert: Japan's Q4 GDP at 0.2% growth with headline CPI at 1.26% and core above 2% alongside a 0.75% policy rate (real rate near 0.5%) signals the BoJ is operating with a negative output gap and disinflation bias. The central bank's guidance that inflation will fall below 2% in late 2026 then rebound toward target in 2027 suggests it sees transitory yen-driven pass-through fading, not structural demand strength.

The BoJ's hold in February and forward guidance of eventual tightening depends entirely on capex and wage growth resilience. The IMF assumes 2.2% inflation for 2026 (above the BoJ's late-year forecast of below 2%), creating optionality: if nominal wages track above 2.5% YoY and capex turns positive, the BoJ can justify 25-50bp of tightening by Q4. If capex remains soft or unemployment edges above 2.5%, expect another year of holds.

Watch April-May earnings season and revised Q1 2026 capex plans for the trigger. If corporate earnings disappoint and firms lower full-year guidance (signaling yen strength concerns and export weakness persist), expect the BoJ to acknowledge slack and delay any tightening signal into 2027 guidance. If earnings and capex beat and wage settlements exceed 2.5%, expect the BoJ to front-load tightening to 1.0% by September rather than hold at 0.75% through year-end.

beginner: Germany just bounced back to growth after two quarters of decline, thanks to people and the government both spending more money.
The government is about to pour cash into infrastructure and military spending, which should keep the economy moving while other European countries are tightening their belts.
Inflation sits at 1.9%, well below the 2.2% forecast, so the central bank has room to keep rates steady without choking off the recovery.
moderate: Germany posted 1.2% growth after two consecutive quarters of contraction, driven by private and public consumption surging at once. This marks a sharp reversal from late 2024 when households pulled back spending.

A new off-budget federal infrastructure fund and rising military expenditure will amplify growth through 2026, offsetting the drag from fiscal consolidation in France and Italy. Germany's budget deficit sits at only 2% of GDP, the healthiest in the eurozone, giving policymakers room to spend.

Core inflation at 1.9% sits below the 2.2% full-year forecast, suggesting base effects are still working in Germany's favor. The unemployment rate of 3.6% remains tight, but wage growth has not yet reignited price pressures.
expert: Q4 GDP acceleration to 1.2% reversed two quarters of decline, with private consumption and government demand both driving the move. The composition matters: public spending is front-loaded and temporary, while private consumption gains rest on subdued wage growth and low real rates, a fragile foundation.

Off-budget infrastructure outlays and military spending (estimated at 2.5% of GDP incrementally) will anchor eurozone growth in 2026 despite French and Italian consolidation, but this support narrows sharply in 2027 as stimulus effects wane and fiscal rules reassert themselves.

CPI inflation tracking 1.9% in February against a 2.2% full-year forecast signals disinflationary momentum persists. Watch the June ECB decision: if core inflation remains anchored below 2%, rate cuts become probable before year-end, accelerating the real-rate decline that backstops consumption gains.

beginner: France's economy is slowing down right now, with activity actually declining in March even as the rest of Europe is still expanding, albeit weakly.
The government has to cut spending to bring down a budget deficit that sits at nearly 5% of GDP, the worst in the eurozone. This fiscal tightening will hold back growth through 2026 and 2027.

Inflation is cooling fast at just 0.9%, giving France the lowest price pressures in the region, but unemployment is stuck at 7.7%, double Germany's rate, so the central bank cannot ease much without risking wage-price spirals.
moderate: March PMI data showed France among the few eurozone countries with declining activity, contrasting sharply with Germany's rebound. The slowdown reflects weak household confidence ahead of fiscal consolidation measures.

A budget deficit of 4.8% forces the government to cut spending, the opposite of Germany's expansionary turn. This creates a two-speed eurozone where German fiscal support in 2026 lifts regional demand, but French households face austerity and weak job creation at the margin.

CPI inflation at 0.9% is the lowest among the four major eurozone economies, but unemployment at 7.7% remains stubbornly high. The combination leaves little room for rate cuts without stoking wage pressure, constraining monetary support for the weakening economy.
expert: March PMI activity indices showed France contracting while the eurozone expanded, signaling France is falling out of step with the region just as German fiscal stimulus kicks in. This divergence will persist through 2026 as fiscal multipliers work against each other.

Budget consolidation targeting a deficit below 4% by 2027 implies structural spending cuts of roughly 1.5% of GDP. Combined with elevated unemployment at 7.7%, this creates a demand drag that will keep GDP growth at 1.4% or below, well below potential.

Core inflation at 0.9% in February, combined with a 4.9% unemployment rate in December, leaves policy rate at 2.15% in real terms at roughly 1.25%. This tight real stance crushes demand during consolidation, forcing a longer, slower adjustment than peers with more fiscal space.

beginner: Italy's economy is weakening right now, with activity dropping in March when most of Europe was still expanding, a bad sign for a country already near stall-speed growth.

The government has to tighten spending to keep the budget deficit under control, which means less room for stimulus. This fiscal squeeze comes just as Germany is loosening, creating an uneven recovery across the eurozone.
Inflation is running at 1.51%, moderate among the region, and unemployment is 5.6%. Italy has breathing room on prices, but weak growth will keep pressure on job creation if consolidation deepens.
moderate: March PMI activity declined in Italy alongside France, indicating both southern eurozone economies are lagging northern peers. Italy's weakness is sharper because the economy was already fragile, with full-year growth forecast at just 1%.

Budget consolidation pressures will force Italy to cut spending to keep the deficit near 3.2% of GDP, tightening fiscal policy precisely when German support is arriving. This creates a structural growth headwind for a country with little cushion on unemployment or productivity.

CPI inflation at 1.51% in February sits below the 2.3% full-year forecast, reflecting persistent slack in the labor market and weak demand. Unemployment at 5.6% is the lowest among the four economies here, but growth forecasts of just 1% for 2026 suggest job creation will stall.
expert: March PMI contracted in Italy, revealing demand deterioration beneath flat headline growth. The 1% full-year GDP forecast assumes no shocks, but consolidation of roughly 1% of GDP adds downside risk if fiscal multipliers exceed consensus expectations.

Italy's budget deficit target of 3.2% GDP implies spending cuts of 1 to 1.5 percentage points of GDP over two years. Paired with a current account surplus of only 0.8% GDP (versus Germany's 4.5%), Italy lacks external offset and will feel consolidation as pure demand destruction.

CPI inflation at 1.51% against a 2.3% full-year forecast indicates significant disinflation momentum, pushing real policy rates (2.15% nominal minus 0.3% expected inflation) above 1.85%. This restrictive stance, combined with fiscal tightening, creates a growth drag extending into 2027 unless eurozone expansion lifts export demand.

beginner: China's economy picked up speed in the last quarter, growing at 4.9%, driven mainly by factories running faster and exports bouncing back after a weak stretch.

The government has already started pumping money into the economy through front-loaded spending, and this boost should keep growth around 5% through 2026 before tapering off as the stimulus effect fades.

Inflation is essentially flat at 0.23%, meaning China still has massive room to cut rates or spend more without stoking price pressures, but the real danger is deflation if excess factories and warehouses continue dumping goods at cut prices.
moderate: Q4 GDP accelerated to 4.9% after two slower quarters, with industrial output and exports leading the rebound. However, this comes on a low base, and the composition reveals reliance on external demand rather than domestic consumption.

Front-loaded fiscal stimulus is supporting 2026 growth, but the boost is concentrated in early quarters and will fade sharply in 2027 as government support normalizes. Full-year GDP growth is forecast at 5% in 2026 then 4.5% in 2027, a 50 basis point deceleration driven purely by policy withdrawal.

CPI inflation at 0.23% in January sits near zero, while the GDP deflator is expected to hover below zero through 2026. This suggests the economy still has excess productive capacity and weak pricing power, a structural constraint that will persist even as fiscal stimulus lifts activity.
expert: Q4 GDP expanded 4.9% driven by industrial production and export gains, but growth remains dependent on external demand and policy support rather than domestic consumption recovery. The composition suggests potential overcapacity in manufacturing persists despite stimulus.

Front-loaded fiscal support concentrated in H1 2026 is expected to generate roughly 100 to 150 basis points of growth uplift, followed by sharp withdrawal in 2027. The full-year forecast of 5% growth in 2026 versus 4.5% in 2027 implies policy stimulus contributes 50 to 100 basis points of the deceleration, not cyclical weakness.

CPI inflation at 0.23% and GDP deflator expected below zero through 2026 signal persistent excess capacity and deflationary bias. Watch producer price inflation (PPI) in coming months: if it remains negative while fiscal stimulus accelerates, pricing power stays absent and real return on government spending declines, forcing larger stimulus outlays to hit growth targets.

beginner: India's growth engine stalled in the last quarter. After roaring ahead at 10.5%, the economy downshifted to 7.3% as businesses cut investment and exports faltered, though Indians kept spending.
Prices barely budged in December at just 1.33%, which means the central bank has room to cut interest rates and give the economy a boost if needed.
The real puzzle is whether this slowdown is temporary or a sign of deeper trouble. Consumption held up, but investment weakness suggests companies are losing confidence.
moderate: India's growth collapsed from 10.5% to 7.3% in Q4 as investment and net trade both deteriorated, a sharp reversal from the torrid pace of the previous quarter. Private consumption stayed resilient, which kept the economy from falling off a cliff.

With inflation at 1.33% in December, the central bank cut rates to 5.25% in January and has room to go further if growth continues slowing. Compare this to the torrid 10.5% growth in Q3, and you see how quickly momentum evaporated.

The forecast calls for 6.3% growth in 2026 despite the recent stumble, betting that private consumption will carry the load as public spending slows. Whether businesses regain appetite for investment will determine if that forecast holds.
expert: GDP deceleration from 10.5% Q3 to 7.3% Q4 driven by gross fixed capital formation contraction and negative net export contribution, though private consumption growth remained positive. This quarter-on-quarter momentum loss signals investment sentiment deterioration.

CPI at 1.33% in December sits well below the 4.2% full-year forecast, triggering the RBI to cut policy rate to 5.25% in January. Real rates have effectively tightened despite headline disinflation, constraining transmission to growth-sensitive segments.

2026 consensus forecast of 6.3% growth assumes consumption-led trajectory absent fiscal stimulus, as public capex growth expected to moderate. Watch capex surveys in Q1 2026 to assess whether private investment responds to the rate cuts or if structural headwinds persist.

beginner: South Africa just got a break on prices. Inflation crashed from nearly 30% last year to under 3% by February, proving that months of brutal interest rate hikes finally worked.

The central bank still has its foot on the brake though, keeping rates at 6.75% because the job is not done yet. Once inflation stays calm for longer, rate cuts could finally start helping the millions of jobless South Africans.

Unemployment at nearly 32% remains catastrophic despite wage recovery starting to boost spending and construction. This recovery is real but fragile, and it will take years to dent the joblessness crisis.
moderate: Inflation plummeted from 29.4% in 2025 to 2.96% in February, a stunning reversal that signals the SARB's aggressive hiking cycle worked. Monthly inflation stabilized around 2% by late 2025, confirming prices are normalizing rather than falling into deflation.

The central bank kept rates at 6.75% in February even as disinflation accelerated, buying time to confirm price stability before cutting. This contrasts sharply with the cutting cycles emerging elsewhere in emerging markets, showing SARB prioritizes durability over growth.

Wage recovery and private investment are reviving consumption and construction, but unemployment at 31.88% remains a structural anchor dragging growth. The 2026 forecast of 3.5% growth depends on these sectoral revivals translating into broader labor absorption.
expert: CPI fell to 2.96% in February from 29.4% YoY in 2025, with monthly inflation stabilized near 2% by Q4 2025, confirming disinflationary trend is durable rather than transitory. Core inflation trajectory suggests space for policy normalization, though SARB held at 6.75% in February.

Real policy rates at 3.79% in February remain restrictive by historical standards, constraining credit growth to consumption and investment despite wage recovery. Energy constraints that amplified inflation shock (via load-shedding) now stabilizing as Eskom generation improvements take hold.

2026 growth forecast of 3.5% assumes consumption acceleration from wage gains and construction rebound drive GDP, but unemployment at 31.88% indicates limited labor market slack to sustain demand. Monitor credit impulse in Q1 2026 to assess whether lower real rates translate to capex acceleration or stall given fiscal constraints.

beginner: Brazil's economy bounced back at the end of last year, growing 0.6% in Q4 as people started spending again and the government opened the wallet. This was a relief after months of stagnation.

The central bank is holding interest rates at 15%, one of the highest in the world, to keep inflation under control at 3.81% in February. That high rate is crushing borrowing and making it harder for businesses to invest.

The trouble ahead is American tariffs. The IMF expects growth to slow to just 1.6% in 2026 partly because the US is raising duties on Brazilian exports, which could derail the recovery that just started.
moderate: GDP grew 0.6% Q4 driven by private and government consumption rebounds, suggesting the worst of the growth crunch may have passed. With inflation at 3.81% in February, cooling from higher levels, this appears to be genuine demand recovery rather than price-driven gains.

The central bank holds rates at 15%, the highest in the EM world, because inflation pressures remain sticky. This puts Brazil in a different policy world than India or South Africa, where rates are already falling. The 15% rate is a direct tax on investment and consumption growth.

US tariff headwinds create a 2026 headwind unique among major EMs. The forecast calls for growth to slow to 1.6%, a dramatic deceleration from recent quarters, driven largely by external demand destruction. Watch export orders surveys closely in Q2 2026 to see if tariff threats become actual demand loss.
expert: GDP rebound of 0.6% in Q4 after prior stagnation driven by household and government consumption recovery, while CPI at 3.81% in February remains above 2026 full-year consensus of 4.2%. Inflation trajectory suggests disinflation is tracking forecasts, but persistence above target justifies continued restrictive stance.

Policy rate anchored at 15.0% in February represents real rate of 11.19%, the most restrictive in major EMs, signaling Banco Central's determination to frontload inflation credibility before external tariff shocks hit demand. This creates policy transmission lag with consumption now responding but capex still depressed.

2026 growth forecast downgraded to 1.6% explicitly citing US tariff impact on exports, creating asymmetric downside risk to consensus. Forward implication: if tariff escalation materializes, central bank may cut rates faster than currently priced, but only after external trade shock becomes undeniable in data (likely Q2 2026 merchandise trade figures).

beginner: Russia is dealing with stubborn inflation at 6.01% in January, well above the central bank's comfort zone. This is the lingering echo of the war in Ukraine, which disrupted global energy markets and made everything from oil to food more expensive.

The central bank jacked rates up to 15.5% in February to fight inflation, one of the highest rates in the world. This aggressive move shows how serious the problem is, even though Russia's economy is smaller now after international sanctions.

Higher oil prices, now assumed at 82 dollars a barrel in 2026, should help Russia's budget and current account. But the economy is not bouncing back the way you might expect from cheaper oil elsewhere, because the damage from the invasion and sanctions is deeper and longer-lasting.
moderate: CPI at 6.01% in January sits significantly above the 4.7% full-year forecast, signaling inflation remains sticky despite the 15.5% policy rate set in February. This persistence reflects supply-side constraints from sanctions and war disruption, not just demand-side overheating.

Russia assumed oil prices of 82.22 dollars in 2026 versus 67.74 in 2025, a 21% jump that should support fiscal and current account balances. But compare this to Canada, where the oil price rebound post-invasion never triggered capex recovery, showing how much structural damage the war has inflicted.

The 2026 forecast calls for just 1.2% growth despite rising oil revenues, revealing how sanctions have throttled the broader economy. Watch Q1 2026 merchandise trade data to see whether higher oil prices are actually flowing through to fiscal revenues or whether export volumes are compressed by logistical constraints.
expert: CPI at 6.01% in January versus 4.7% full-year consensus suggests disinflationary trajectory is slower than expected, likely reflecting ruble depreciation pass-through from geopolitical risk premium and goods-side constraints from sanctions. Central bank's 15.5% rate in February represents real policy rate of 9.49%, the highest among major commodity exporters.

Brent crude assumption at 82.22 dollars in 2026 (versus 67.74 in 2025) improves Russia's fiscal and external position, but GDP forecast of 1.2% growth implies elasticity to oil prices has collapsed relative to historical norms, revealing depth of structural productive capacity loss from sanctions.

Forward implication: Russia's external balance (2% surplus forecast) remains dependent on sustained elevated oil prices and continued import compression from sanctions, not supply-side recovery. If Brent falls below 75 dollars in H1 2026, inflation-adjusted fiscal space contracts sharply, forcing either rate cuts (reigniting inflation) or spending cuts (accelerating growth deceleration).
